title: Elisha's Last Arrow and the Grace That Held Israel
summary: Two kings of Jehu's line, Jehoahaz and his son Jehoash, rule the northern kingdom while Aram grinds Israel down. Jehoahaz pleads with the LORD and a deliverer is given, though the nation keeps the old sins. The dying Elisha has Jehoash shoot an arrow of victory and strike the ground, a dead man revives at the touch of the prophet's bones, and the chapter closes with the LORD's compassion for the sake of his covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.
story: Jehu had wiped out the house of Ahab and the Baal cult in Samaria (chapters 9 and 10), and Joash of Judah had repaired the temple after Athaliah's fall (chapters 11 and 12). Now the story returns to the north, where Jehu's dynasty holds the throne but the golden calves of Jeroboam still stand. The chapter does two things at once. It shows Israel at its weakest under Aramean pressure, and it closes the long Elisha cycle that began when the mantle fell from Elijah in chapter 2. Elisha dies, yet even his grave gives life, and the chapter ends not with judgment but with the LORD refusing, for now, to cast Israel away. That mercy sets up the recovery under Jeroboam II in chapter 14 and makes the final fall in chapter 17 all the more sobering.
historical:
Jehoahaz reigned in Samaria from about 814 to 798 BC and his son Jehoash (also spelled Joash) from about 798 to 782 BC; the exact figures depend on how scholars reconcile the book's synchronisms with Judah. Their enemy was Hazael of Damascus, the usurper Elisha had wept over in 8:7-15, and after him his son Ben-hadad. Aram-Damascus was at the height of its power in these decades, and the figure of fifty horsemen, ten chariots, and ten thousand foot soldiers (verse 7) shows how far Israel had fallen from the chariot army Ahab once fielded.

The relief came in part from outside. The Assyrian king Adad-nirari III campaigned west at the end of the ninth century and forced Damascus to pay tribute, which broke Aram's grip on Israel. An Assyrian stela found at Tell al-Rimah in northern Iraq names Joash of Samaria among the kings who paid Adad-nirari tribute. Many scholars think the unnamed deliverer of verse 5 is Adad-nirari, working unknowingly as the LORD's instrument; others identify the deliverer with Jehoash himself, who recovered the cities in verse 25, or with Jeroboam II, whom 14:27 describes as the one through whom the LORD saved Israel.
cultural:
Two gestures in the Elisha scene belonged to the world of ancient war and prophecy. Shooting an arrow toward enemy territory was a known way of opening a campaign, and the east window pointed across the Jordan toward the Aramean lands where Aphek lay. Elisha's hands on the king's hands mark the arrow as the LORD's, not the king's. The second act, striking the ground with the arrows, is a prophetic sign-act: a physical action that embodies and sets in motion what God has said. The king's half-hearted three strikes reveal the limits of his expectation, and the prophet reads them as the limit of the victory.

The king's cry, “My father, my father, the chariots and horsemen of Israel!” (verse 14), repeats Elisha's own words as Elijah was taken up (2:12). "Father" was a title of honor for a prophet who led a band of disciples. The phrase about chariots and horsemen named the prophet as Israel's real defense, worth more than the army Aram had destroyed. Burial customs also stand behind verse 21: families used rock-cut tombs reused for several bodies, which is why a burial party could hurry a corpse into a tomb that was already occupied.
literary: The chapter is built from the regular formulas of Kings: an opening synchronism with Judah's king, a verdict ("he did evil in the sight of the LORD"), a reference to the royal annals, and a burial notice. Twice that frame is laid down (verses 1-9 and 10-13), and the burial of Jehoash is reported before the story of his visit to Elisha, which is told out of chronological order so that the prophet's death can close the section. Verses 3-5 follow the pattern of the book of Judges: sin, oppression, a cry to the LORD, a deliverer, rest. Verses 22-25 then gather up the Aram story, with the covenant statement of verse 23 standing at the center as the narrator's explanation of everything around it. The number three runs through the ending: three strikes, three victories.

outline.t: Jehoahaz: oppression, a plea, and a deliverer
The dying Elisha and the arrows of victory
Elisha's death and the man revived in his tomb
Covenant compassion and three victories over Aram

doctrines.note: Verse 23 gives the reason Israel survives: the LORD turned toward them because of his covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Israel's endurance rests on God's promise, not on the nation's faithfulness, which the chapter says plainly was lacking.
God answers Jehoahaz by raising up a deliverer, very possibly a foreign king who had no idea whose purpose he served. Kings rule the nations, but history moves under God's hand.
The arrows show that the promise was generous and the king's grasp of it small. Faith here means expecting what God has said, and Jehoash's three strikes show a man content with too little.

words.note: Teshuah, deliverance or victory. Elisha calls the arrow the arrow of the LORD's victory. The word is used across the Old Testament for rescue that comes from God, and it is close kin to the name Joshua and, through it, the name Jesus. Here it insists that Israel's victories over Aram are the LORD's saving acts.

Berit, covenant: a binding relationship with promises and obligations. This is the only time in the chapter the word appears, and it carries the weight of the whole ending. The covenant with the patriarchs, older than the kingdom and older than the law at Sinai, holds Israel when the nation has broken faith.

Racham, to have compassion. The verb is related to the Hebrew word for womb, and it describes a deep, tender pity, the love of a parent for a child. Set beside "gracious" in verse 23, it tells us how God looks at the people he is about to rescue.

christ: The chapter's clearest pointer forward is the man revived by touching Elisha's bones. It does not predict Jesus, but it belongs to a pattern the Bible builds: the LORD gives life where there is only death, through his servants and finally through his Son. Elijah and Elisha each raised the dead (1 Kings 17 and 2 Kings 4), and here life flows even from a prophet's grave. The New Testament goes further, proclaiming that Jesus did not merely give life from a tomb but walked out of his own, the firstborn from the dead. The covenant mercy of verse 23 points forward too: Mary's song in Luke 1 praises God for remembering his mercy to Abraham and his descendants in sending the Messiah. God's refusal to cast Israel from his presence, for the sake of the patriarchs, is the same faithfulness that brings Christ into the world.

hard.q: Is the story of Elisha's bones a kind of magic, and why was Elisha angry at a king who did what he was told?
hard.a:
The revival in verse 21 is told briefly and without comment. Some readers have taken it as support for venerating the remains of holy people, a practice with a long history in parts of the church. Others note that the text shows no one seeking out the bones, praying to Elisha, or keeping them as a relic; the man was thrown in by frightened mourners, and the power belongs to the LORD, who confirms that the word Elisha spoke is still alive after his death. Either way, the story doesn't make the bones a tool people can use.

Elisha's anger in verse 19 can seem unfair, since he never told the king how many times to strike. But the sign-act tested what the king expected. Jehoash had just heard that the LORD would give victory over Aram until it was finished; striking three times and stopping showed a man who wanted a little relief rather than the full deliverance promised. The fault lay not in failing to guess a number but in the smallness of his hope.

questions: Jehoash struck the ground three times and stopped. Where do you settle for a smaller portion of what God has promised than he has offered?
Israel survived not because it repented but because God remembered his covenant with Abraham. How does that shape the way you think about God's patience with you?
Jehoash wept at Elisha's bedside yet kept the calves of Jeroboam. What does it look like to honor God's servants while refusing to change?
